notes: The poet as carpenter of words (West 2007 ch. 1; Watkins 1995 ch. 5; formula craft-words): Ved. vácāṃsi ... takṣam 'I have fashioned words (for him)', Av. vacas-tašti- 'fashioning of utterance' (a Gathic strophe), Gk ἐπέων ... τέκτονες 'carpenters of verses'. Both roots, *wekʷ-os 'word' (Ved. vácas- = Gk ἔπος) and *tetḱ- 'fashion' (takṣ-, taš-, τέκτων), are shared. Vedic takṣam is an aorist injunctive; the lexicon has only the present of *tetḱ-, used here. 'For him' (Ved. asmai) is interpolated.

Pindar's 'carpenters of words' (ἐπέων τέκτονες) beside the Vedic poet who fashions his song 'like a carpenter' (táṣṭeva, RV 3.38.1, 1.61.4) and the Avestan vacas-tašti-. Gk τέκτων = Ved. tákṣan- (*tétḱō); the Vedic passages have the agent noun táṣṭar- of the same root, so the match is at root level. 'Word' as in poetics-gifts-001 (Gk ἐπέων, Av. vacas-). The simile 'like' has no usable particle and the 1st plural copula is interpolated.

Poetry as weaving (West 2007 ch. 1): Av. vaf- 'weave' > 'hymn' (Y. 28.3 ufiiānī 'I will hymn'), Gk ὑφαίνω with ὕμνον (Bacchylides), OE wordcræft wæf 'I wove word-craft'; all *(h₁)webʰ-. The lexicon offers only derived presents of the root; the thematic wébʰeti (as OE wefan) is used, gloss approximate. The object is not shared (Gk ὕμνος, OE wordcræft): 'words' (wékʷos) is interpolated. Ved. váy-/ūvuḥ 'weave' (RV 1.61.8) is another root and is not cited.

cognate_refs.locus: Ion of Chios fr. 27.7; Eur. Phaethon 101

notes: The song sent on its way with the 3sg imperative of 'go': Ved. prá ... etu (RV 1.154.3 mánma, 7.34.1 manīṣā́, 7.66.1 stómaḥ naḥ 'our praise') and Gk ἴτω ἀοιδή (West 2007 ch. 1). etu = ἴτω (*h₁éytu). The subject is renewed in each tradition (stóma-, mánman-, ἀοιδή); 'word' (wékʷos) is interpolated, as are pró (Vedic only) and 'our' (Ved. naḥ).

The song flies (*peth₂-): RV 1.25.4 'forth fly my thoughts' (pátanti), Homer's ἔπεα πτερόεντα 'winged words', Aeschylus' prayer that 'flies forth' (ποτάσθω) (West 2007 ch. 1). The verb root is shared (Ved. pátanti, Gk πτερ-όεντα, ποτά-); 'words' is the Greek noun (ἔπεα), the Vedic has vímanyavaḥ 'thoughts', so wékʷos is marked interpolated. A neuter plural subject takes a singular verb. 'Forth' (pró) stands for Ved. párā (interpolated); 'my' for Ved. me.

Poetry as recall, root *men- (West 2007 ch. 1): the Sibyl's 'ancient tales ... that I remember' and 'I remember (ek man) the giants' (Vsp. 1–2, confirmed in the local Edda), the Beowulf thane 'mindful of songs' who 'remembered' (gemunde) a multitude of old stories (confirmed locally), the Muses who 'would recall' (μνησαίατο, confirmed in the treebank), and the Vedic poets who 'think out' a praise (manāmahe). ON man and OE gemunan are preterite-presents, continuing the perfect *memón- (memóne); the Greek and Vedic forms are other stems of the root, so the match is root-level. 'Old words' renders forn spjöll / eald-gesegena: sénos and wékʷos are interpolated.

plan.english: The gods are givers of good things.

notes: 'Givers of good things' (Benfey; West 2007 ch. 3): Gk θεοὶ δωτῆρες ἐάων (Od. 8.325, Hes. Th. 46), Av. vohunąm dātārō of the Aməša Spəṇtas (Y. 65.12, confirmed locally), Ved. dātā́ vásūnām (RV 8.51.5, of Indra). Agent noun of *deh₃- with the genitive plural of *h₁wésu- 'good' used as a noun; the Greek ἐάων is the archaic genitive plural of ἐΰς. 'Gods' (deywós; Gk θεοί is not cognate) and the copula are interpolated.

plan.english: We sacrifice to the giver of good things.

notes: The same epithet as the object of worship: Y. 16.1 'we worship ... Ahura Mazdā, giver of good things' (dātārəm vohunąm yazamaide, confirmed locally), RV 8.51.5 'who is our giver of goods, that Indra we call', Od. 8.335 Hermes addressed as δῶτορ ἑάων. The verb is the Avestan middle yazamaide (Ved. yajāmahe), h₁yáǵeti 'sacrifice (to)' with the accusative of the deity as in Indo-Iranian; it is Indo-Iranian only, interpolated.

plan.english: I heard: he gives no horses for songs; he gives a cow.

notes: The 'inverse dānastuti' (Watkins 1995: 187): the Irish quatrain (ro-cúala ... eochu ar dúana ... bó: 'I have heard he gives no horses for poems ... a cow'), whose frame ro-cúala 'I have heard' is the exact cognate of Vedic śuśrava (*ḱuḱlowh₂a) in praise of generosity (RV 1.109.2, 5: áśravam 'I heard you give more plentifully'); horses and cows are the canonical gifts of the Vedic dānastuti (RV 1.126.2 a hundred horses, cows). Ved. áśvān / OIr eochu, gónām / bó. The aorist follows Vedic áśravam (the OIr is a perfect). 'Give' is interpolated: OIr do-beir is *bʰer-, Vedic has dā-; dédeh₃ti chosen. 'Songs' (OIr dúana) is interpolated with kéh₂nmn̥ 'song'.

plan.english: He gave horses for the song.

notes: Horses as the poet's fee for a song: RV 6.63.10 'Purupantha gave hundreds, thousands of horses for the song' (gíre dāt, Watkins 1995: 74), Y. 44.18 the promised reward of ten mares, and the Irish complaint that a mean patron gives 'no horses for poems' (eochu ar dúana). Horse is shared by three traditions (two branches). The verb is the Vedic root aorist dāt (déh₃t; the OIr has do-beir), interpolated; 'song' (Ved. gír-, OIr dúan, not cognate) is interpolated with kéh₂nmn̥, a dative of purpose as in Vedic gíre.

plan.english: Those who gave me horses, make great fame for them!

notes: Gift and counter-gift (Watkins 1995 ch. 5): in the dānastuti of RV 5.18.5 the poet asks Agni to make 'great fame' (máhi śrávaḥ) for the patrons who gave him fifty horses; 'great fame' máhi śrávaḥ = Gk μέγα κλέος (Il. 6.446, confirmed in the treebank; West 2007 ch. 10). Relative clause first, then the correlative, as in the Vedic. 'Fifty' has no numeral in the closed set and is left out; the verbs (Ved. dadúḥ, kṛdhi = root aorists of *deh₃- and *kʷer-) and 'horses' are Vedic only here, interpolated.

Kuhn's equation śrávaḥ ákṣitam = κλέος ἄφθιτον (RV 1.9.7, Il. 9.413, both confirmed locally), here in the poet's request on behalf of his patrons (RV 1.9.7 'set on us ... imperishable fame') and in Ibycus' pledge to Polycrates that he will have κλέος ἄφθιτον through the poet's song (Watkins 1995: 70; West 2007 ch. 10). The verb dʰeh₁ (Ved. dhehi) and 'on us' (asmé, rendered by the dative enclitic) are Vedic only, interpolated; Vedic also has pṛthú and bṛhát, left out.

'Good fame' *h₁wésu ḱléwos: Av. vohu sravah- (Y. 30.10 vaŋhāu srauuahī, confirmed locally) and OIr fó chlú, beside the compounds Ved. suśrávas-, Gk εὐκλεής, OIr sochla (West 2007 ch. 10; Homer renews the phrase as κλέος ἐσθλόν). The wish form (optative of the copula with a dative of possession) is interpolated; Avestan has a locative 'in good fame'.

plan.english: How shall I win the reward, ten horses?

notes: The poet's fee *misdʰó- (Benveniste; Watkins 1995: 71): Zarathustra asks how he shall win his reward (mīždəm hanānī), ten mares with a stallion and a camel (Y. 44.18, confirmed locally); Pindar 'will win' the Athenians' gratitude as his μισθός (Pyth. 1.75–77). Only 'reward' is shared. The Avestan aorist subjunctive hanānī (*senh₂-, = Ved. san- 'win') gives the verb and mood (interpolated); 'ten' and 'horses' are Avestan only (aspā̊ is feminine 'mares'; the masculine h₁éḱwos is used), interpolated; 'how' renders kaϑā with kʷíh₁ (interpolated).

The singer's or suppliant's opening demand for a hearing: Gk κλῦθί μευ (Il. 1.37, confirmed in the treebank) = Ved. śrudhī (RV 1.25.19 imáṃ me ... śrudhī hávam), both the root-aorist imperative *ḱlu-dʰí; the Sibyl's 'hearing I ask' (hljóðs, *ḱleu-to-) opens Vǫluspá (confirmed locally; West 2007 ch. 2). The Greek and Vedic pronouns are genitive/dative enclitics; the engine's accusative enclitic is used (interpolated, closed class).
